readerTitle: Being first only buys you time
caseNote: 가상 사례 2개 (리필 매장, 히트펌프 설치 업체) + 가상 적용 (물리치료 클리닉용 소프트웨어) + 실제 연구 (Lieberman & Montgomery 1988, Golder & Tellis 1993)
insight: 먼저 들어가는 것 자체는 시간을 버는 것일 뿐이다. 그 시간을 경쟁자가 쉽게 가져갈 수 없는 것(희소 자원, 전환 비용, 학습 우위)으로 바꿔야 우위가 된다.
misconception: 시장에 먼저 들어가기만 하면 자연히 1등 자리를 지킬 수 있다.

sources.text: Lieberman, M. B., & Montgomery, D. B. (1988). First-Mover Advantages. Strategic Management Journal, 9(S1), 41–58.
Golder, P. N., & Tellis, G. J. (1993). Pioneer Advantage: Marketing Logic or Marketing Legend? Journal of Marketing Research, 30(2), 158–170.
리필 매장, 히트펌프 설치 업체, 클리닉 소프트웨어 사례는 설명용 가상 사례

factChecks.note: Lieberman & Montgomery(1988)가 제시한 선발자 우위의 원천(기술 리더십·학습, 희소 자원 선점, 구매자 전환 비용)을 카드 6에서 쉬운 말로 세 가지로 요약했습니다. 원문 분류와 표현이 맞는지 확인하세요.
Golder & Tellis(1993)는 약 50개 제품 범주의 역사를 추적해 많은 개척 기업이 실패했고 이후 진입자가 리더가 되는 경우가 많았다고 보고했습니다. 구체적 수치(실패율, 평균 점유율)는 확인 전이라 카드에 넣지 않았고 'dozens of product categories'로만 적었습니다.
네트워크 효과는 Lieberman & Montgomery(1988)의 원래 분류에 명시된 항목이 아니므로 softwareNote에서 연구 인용 없이 일반 원리로만 설명했습니다.
카드 3·4의 두 사업과 카드 8의 소프트웨어 사례는 모두 가상이며 수치를 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Both were first. Only one stayed ahead.
body: Two owners did the same thing in the same year. Each opened the first business of its kind in their area.
Five years later, one leads its market comfortably. The other is fighting a supermarket and a copycat shop for the same customers. Being first wasn't the difference. What they did with it was.

image.label: Two shopfronts, one busy, one surrounded by new rivals
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 왼쪽은 작은 리필 매장 하나가 새로 생긴 대형 마트와 다른 가게 사이에 끼어 있는 모습, 오른쪽은 작업 밴과 기술자들이 줄지어 선 난방 설비 업체. 두 가게 모두 'FIRST' 깃발을 달고 있음. 실제 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: You'll be first. Rivals will follow.
body: You're opening your town's first refill shop, where customers bring their own jars for soap, pasta and oil. You expect a rival within a year or two.
Where should your head start go?

options.text: Heavy marketing to become known as *the original*
options.feedback: Awareness helps early. But a label alone rarely stops customers from trying a closer or cheaper shop once one opens.

options.text: Lock in something a rival can't easily get, like the best location on a long lease or an exclusive local supplier
options.feedback: It costs more up front and commits you for years. In return, the rival arrives to find the best spot and supplier already taken.

options.text: Stay small and cheap until you know demand is real
options.feedback: This protects your cash if the idea flops. But it spends the head start on caution and leaves the best assets open for whoever comes next.

cards.title: The refill shop: first, loved, then crowded.
body: The refill shop opened on a side street with a month-to-month lease. Local press covered it. Regulars loved it.
In year two, a supermarket added a refill aisle, and a second shop opened on the high street. Nothing held customers in place. Their jars worked anywhere, and the new options were closer.
Sales dropped sharply. The shop had been first, but it owned nothing a rival couldn't match.

cards.title: The heat-pump installer: first, then hard to catch.
body: A home-heating firm became the first in its region to install heat pumps. Trained technicians were scarce, so it hired and trained most of them.
It sold every install with a yearly service plan. Each job taught the team something, and happy customers sent referrals.
When rivals arrived, they couldn't find trained staff, and existing customers stayed for their servicing.

image.label: Two timelines: one head start fades, one grows
image.brief: 두 개의 가로 타임라인 비교. 위쪽 'Refill shop' 줄은 'Opened first' 다음에 경쟁자 아이콘이 나타나며 막대가 줄어듦. 아래쪽 'Installer' 줄은 'Opened first' 다음에 'Trained staff', 'Service plans', 'Referrals' 아이콘이 쌓이며 막대가 커짐. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: First-mover advantage
body: **First-mover advantage** is the edge a business gains by entering a market before its rivals.
But being first only buys you time. The advantage is what you build with that time before others show up.
The refill shop spent its time being popular. The installer spent it building things rivals couldn't quickly copy.

cards.title: Three ways a head start becomes hard to take.
body: Economists Marvin Lieberman and David Montgomery described the main sources of first-mover advantage in 1988. Put simply:
list: **Scarce assets:** the best locations, suppliers, staff or permits, taken before others arrive
**Switching costs:** contracts, stored history or habits that make leaving a hassle for customers
**Learning lead:** more jobs done means lower costs and better work than a newcomer can offer
cards.callout: If your head start doesn't turn into at least one of these, it fades once rivals come.
cards.softwareNote: Software often adds a fourth: network effects, where each new user makes the product more valuable to others. A marketplace with the most buyers attracts the most sellers, which is hard for a later entrant to break.

cards.title: Being first is also expensive.
body: First movers pay to teach customers what the product even is. They guess at what people want and make mistakes that followers can watch and avoid for free.

In a well-known 1993 study, Peter Golder and Gerard Tellis traced the history of dozens of product categories. They found that many market pioneers had failed, and that market leaders had often entered later. Being first is a chance, not a prize.

image.label: A trailblazer clearing a path while others follow easily
image.brief: 정글 길을 칼로 힘들게 개척하는 사람 뒤로, 이미 닦인 길을 편하게 걸어오는 사람들. 단순한 플랫 일러스트, 따뜻한 색감. 텍스트 없음.

cards.title: Now it's software for clinics.
body: You've built the first booking and billing tool for small physiotherapy clinics in your country. You expect a bigger software company to copy it within a year.
How should you use that year?

options.text: Add as many features as possible to stay ahead
options.feedback: Features help you win deals now. But a well-funded rival can copy features fast, so they rarely hold a lead on their own.

options.text: Move each clinic's records and schedules in for them, and connect to local insurers' billing
options.feedback: It's slow, unglamorous work. But clinics with years of records inside your tool and billing that just works have real reasons not to switch.

options.text: Offer it nearly free to sign up every clinic fast
options.feedback: You'd grow quickly, but cheap sign-ups with nothing tying them to you can leave just as fast when a rival offers the same deal.

cards.title: Being first buys time. Spend it on what lasts.
body: A head start only matters if it turns into something rivals can't quickly get: scarce assets, customers who'd find it hard to leave, or a learning lead.
**Try it today:** list what you have that a new competitor couldn't copy within a year. If the list is just *we were here first*, pick one item to build this quarter.
